3. It appears from the impugned order that the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the plaintiffs aforesaid application dated 12.10.89 not on merit, but on the ground that it was not maintainable. The learned Subordinate Judge obviously thought that an order rejecting a plaint being a decree the proper remedy for the plaintiff was to file an appeal or to file a fresh suit. 

 4. Though according to definition in section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure an order rejecting a plaint is a decree and, as such, appeal lies against thereof, but proper relief in an appeal can be given on scrutiny of the propriety of the order rejecting a plaint if it is passed either under clause (a) or (d) of rule 11 of Order 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In case of rejection of plaint under clause (b) or (c) it is difficult to get relief in an appeal, like the instant case, when a plaint is rejected for not supplying the requisite stamp papers within a time fixed by the court as in such a case impugned order must be found to be a proper one. But if there is sufficient cause for not supplying the same within the time fixed we hold that restoration of the plaint may be ordered in appropriate cases on an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. After all, procedure is the machinery whereby justice reaches and therefore it must be such as can facilitate justice.
